title: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
desc: Associates the GenAI era with self-representation but not causation or improved outcomes, while distinguishing provider augmentation.

kps.k: The central question is whether cheaper legal assistance delivers effective remedies, not merely more information or filings.
kps.d: The cluster distinguishes three routes to wider access: consumer self-help, greater legal-aid capacity and redesigned court processes. The ABA’s 2024 report grounds their promise in the Legal Services Corporation’s estimate that 92% of low-income Americans’ substantial civil legal problems receive no or inadequate help. That measures unmet problems, not the proportion of people unable to obtain representation. Bibas argues that bespoke representation cannot economically serve many small-dollar matters; Fines, drawing on Sandefur, stresses that people also fail to recognise their problems as legal. These accounts imply that lowering prices alone may not address the justice gap.

qs.q: The Legal Services Corporation estimates that 92 percent of the substantial civil legal    problems of low-income Americans receive no or inadequate help.
qs.a: ABA Task Force on Law and Artificial Intelligence — Year 1 Report on the Impact of AI on the Practice of Law (August 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Legal technology driven by artificial intelligence (AI) has been heralded for its potential to combat these challenges on three access-to-justice fronts that are often conceptualized in isolation: a consumer (i.e., self-help) front, a legal-service-provider front, and a court front.
qs.a: Interoperable Legal AI for Access to Justice · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Federal filing studies associate the generative-AI era with more self-representation, but do not establish that AI caused the increase.
kps.d: Cohen-Sasson’s The New Pro Se analyses approximately 2.8 million FY2008–2025 filings and reports a rise from 11.33% before widespread GenAI access to 16.94% afterward. Artificial Access to Justice reports 22.3% in the final quarter of FY2025; that endpoint is not interchangeable with the post-period average, and the overlapping Cohen-Sasson material should not count as independent replication. Shah and Levy analyse roughly 4.6 million non-prisoner federal civil cases across FY2005–FY2026 and report a 16.8% pro se share in FY2025, with growth concentrated in document-driven categories. Cohen-Sasson does not directly observe individual AI use; Shah and Levy’s supplied validation passage omits its substantive result. Neither timing nor textual drafting flags alone establishes causation or lawyer displacement.

qs.a: The New Pro Se: Generative AI and the Surge in Federal Civil Self-Representation · Academia · 2026

qs.q: First, the national non-prisoner pro se filing share rose sharply from its approximately 11% historical steady state to 16.8% in fiscal year 2025, a gain that has no precedent in 25 years of administrative records.
qs.a: Access to Justice in the Age of AI: Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts · Academia · 2026

kps.k: More polished complaints and greater participation do not yet demonstrate better legal outcomes.
kps.d: Cohen-Sasson reports that AI-flagged complaints face more dismissals, terminate earlier and prevail no more frequently than their comparison group. Shah and Levy instead find no faster resolution and little apparent change in case quality from disposition patterns. These findings concern different comparisons, so they are not a direct contradiction. Cohen-Sasson proposes marginal-case entry, superficial compliance with pleading standards and AI-reinforced overconfidence, but cannot separate those mechanisms. His doctrinal account also proposes a polish penalty when professional-looking text reduces judicial solicitude. Distributional gains remain uncertain: first-time filers feature disproportionately among flagged complaints, but their 27.3% fee-waiver share versus 24.4% for unflagged complaints is not significantly different.

qs.q: Second, cases are not resolving any faster and analysis of case disposition suggests little change in the quality of cases brought by pro se litigants.
qs.a: Access to Justice in the Age of AI: Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts · Academia · 2026

qs.q: The most striking misfire is the polish penalty: the solicitude ordinarily afforded an untrained litigant is withheld because her complaint reads too well.
qs.a: Artificial Access to Justice: AI and the Surge in Pro Se Litigation · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Lower drafting costs may transfer work to courts rather than reduce total institutional burdens.
kps.d: Shah and Levy report that aggregate pro se docket entries per court within cases’ first 180 days increased 64% on average in Q4 2022–Q2 2025 relative to the pre-AI mean, reaching 158% above that mean in Q2 2025. These figures measure aggregate volume, not activity per individual case. Cohen-Sasson argues that weakened pre-filing filters shift screening to judges, staff and defendants, even without formal court adoption of AI. By contrast, McCormack’s account in the Year 2 report anticipates shorter dockets and more accessible dispute resolution through automation and agents. Those prospective benefits are not measured counterevidence to the federal workload findings and concern a different deployment setting.

qs.q: Since the advent of capable LLMs, the total volume of pro se docket entries per court in the first 180 days of a case has grown by 64% on average across the post-AI period (Q4 2022–Q2 2025), and by 2025Q2—the most recent fully observable quarter at the 180-day horizon—this volume has more than doubled (+158%) the pre-AI mean.
qs.a: Access to Justice in the Age of AI: Evidence from U.S. Federal Courts · Academia · 2026

qs.q: The screening that AI displaces does not disappear; it migrates to the docket, burdening judges, staff, and defendants.
qs.a: Artificial Access to Justice: AI and the Surge in Pro Se Litigation · Academia · 2026

kps.k: Provider augmentation offers a distinct pathway, but practical examples do not establish population-level access gains.
kps.d: Chien and Kim reason that increasing oversubscribed legal-aid workers’ productivity could expand assistance; their supplied excerpts do not contain the field-study results. Markovic separately reports their intake and drafting findings as encouraging. Access to Justice 2.0 illustrates subsidised software and consumer tools, while the 2025 access-to-justice report presents applications and contributor recommendations without complete quantified outcomes. Adjacent criminal-defense research provides task-specific interview evidence: 17 public defense professionals saw greatest potential in evidence investigation and least compatibility with courtroom representation and strategy. Its recommendations favour collaboration, defender-specific benchmarks and local deployment, not autonomous replacement of counsel.

qs.q: 9 Legal aid services are often oversubscribed, addressing only a fraction of the need, implying that increasing the productivity of legal aid profession- als could appreciably increase access to justice.
qs.a: Generative AI and Legal Aid: Results from a Field Study and 100 Use Cases to Bridge the Access to Justice Gap · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Simultaneously, initiatives such as Thomson Reuters' AI for Justice Legal Aid program and Everlaw for Good are helping bridge the access-to-justice gap by providing legal aid organizations and nonprofits with cost-effective access to advanced AI tools.
qs.a: Access to Justice 2.0: How AI-Powered Software Can Bridge the Gap · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The distributional dispute concerns who captures AI’s benefits and who bears its errors and litigation costs.
kps.d: Simshaw distinguishes risks that poorer users receive inferior AI, only expensive firms harness it effectively, or affordability barriers remain unchanged. Markovic adds an adversarial mechanism: cheaper claim initiation could expand debt and rent litigation against underserved people, potentially worsening their position even if they adopt AI. That remains a conditional prediction, not an observed effect established here. Digital access, literacy, distrust and inability to recognise legal needs further qualify universal-access claims. Sonday’s contribution to the 2025 report extends the concern to unequal capacity among legal-aid organisations, arguing that low software prices do not replace targeted funding and shared infrastructure.

qs.q: But some fear that increased reliance on AI will lead to one or more two-tiered systems: the poor might be stuck with inferior AI-driven assistance; only expensive law firms might be able to effectively harness legal AI; or, AI’s impact might not disrupt the status quo where only some can afford any type of legal assistance.
qs.a: Access to A.I. Justice: Avoiding an Inequitable Two-Tiered System of Legal Services · Academia · 2022

qs.q: plaintiff” such as a financial institution seeking to recover a debt or back rent from a self-represented litigant.56 As the cost of initiating legal actions approaches zero, AI may well lead to more disputes and more assembly-line litigation against low- and middle-income people.
qs.a: Equal Justice and Generative AI · Academia · 2025

kps.k: Human verification is a substantive access constraint, not a safeguard that every consumer can readily perform.
kps.d: The small-value consumer-claims analysis argues that drafting and brainstorming do not necessarily help users identify their claims, and that consumers may lack time or expertise to check accuracy. Markovic similarly links information asymmetry to exposure to fabricated or misleading output. Berkenkotter and Lipinsky cite persistent fabricated citations in specialised tools and litigation incidents involving both lawyers and self-represented parties; these incidents illustrate consequences rather than model error rates. Proposed responses include trained justice tech workers, reasonable checking of factual and legal claims, court-provided AI literacy and free legal information. These proposals seek to make verification feasible rather than rely solely on warnings or sanctions.

qs.q: Summarising, drafting and brainstorming16 are not the assistance required by consumers unaware even of what their claim may be and how best to pursue it.
qs.a: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Small Value Consumer Claims: Hallucination Risk, System Design, and Governance in Online Dispute Resolution · Academia · 2025

qs.q: But according to researchers at Stanford, even those generative AI tools have not completely eliminated the inclusion of hallucinated legal citations in outputs.
qs.a: Can Robot Lawyers Close the Access to Justice Gap? · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: Regulatory proposals differ over how to enable assistance while protecting users, rather than simply dividing into pro- and anti-AI positions.
kps.d: Walters and Fines favour revisiting unauthorized-practice restrictions while retaining protection against negligent or fraudulent assistance; Walters insists that consumer protection also account for receiving no help. Bibas emphasises lighter bar regulation and simpler procedures. Bonardi and Branting outline certification and exemptions for certified assistants, but the supplied material does not specify operational thresholds or establish effectiveness. Simshaw supports regulated experimentation and context-specific design. Legal Market Decartelization rejects deregulation as an exclusive strategy, favouring targeted barriers, legal-aid investment, education and process reform. The substantive disagreement concerns the scope and priority of reform, not whether safeguards matter.

qs.q: Considering the potential benefit to consumers, state legislatures should re-evaluate the scope of UPL laws in order to expand assistance while still protecting consumers from negligent or fraudulent legal services.
qs.a: Re-Regulating UPL in an Age of AI · Academia · 2024

qs.q: By relaxing UPL restrictions and encouraging collaboration between attorneys and AI developers, the legal system can balance consumer protection with innovation, ensuring that AI serves as a tool to expand access to justice.
qs.a: AI, UPL, & A2J: Generative AI's Disruptions in the Delivery of Legal Services to Low-Income Individuals · Academia · 2025

kps.k: The practical agenda shifts from isolated tools to coordinated, user-centred legal assistance and court adaptation.
kps.d: Simshaw recommends court-led technological and procedural interoperability across consumers, providers and courts. Stanford Legal Design Lab material calls for community interviews and design research to counterbalance expert assumptions about users’ interests. Cohen-Sasson favours staff training, triage and filing policies rather than prohibiting litigant AI use. The 2025 report includes staged deployment from staff-facing tools to consumer services with human fallback, current legal data and independent testing. These remain reform agendas, not demonstrated solutions. Much of the remaining supplied material consists only of references; it adds no independent outcome, benchmark or reliability findings to this cluster.

qs.q: This Essay argues that technological and procedural legal interoperability—that is, widespread consistency in technology design and related processes—should be at the forefront of these efforts, particularly as they relate to artificial intelligence.
qs.a: Interoperable Legal AI for Access to Justice · Academia · 2025

qs.q: These empirical findings provide directions that can counterbalance legal domain experts’ proposals about the public interest around AI, as expressed by attorneys, court officials, advocates, and regulators.
qs.a: AI & Access to Justice Initiative — project hub (Stanford Legal Design Lab) · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: The substantive academia-and-research sources generally accept the proposition’s central distinction: cheaper or more accessible AI assistance may increase information, drafting and filings without producing effective remedies. They materially develop it through several forms of evidence and argument. Federal-court studies associate the GenAI period with increased self-representation but stop short of establishing causation; Cohen-Sasson adds complaint-level evidence of worse or unchanged outcomes and a proposed transfer of screening work to judges, staff and defendants, while Shah and Levy report increased docket activity without faster resolution or clear quality gains. Other researchers extend the proposition through distributional and institutional analysis: unequal digital access, inability to recognise legal problems, limited capacity for human verification, and sophisticated opponents’ use of AI may prevent or reverse access gains. Provider-side research identifies augmentation of legal-aid workers and public defenders as a distinct pathway, with task-specific limits rather than autonomous replacement. The principal internal variation concerns remedies rather than the core diagnosis: proposals range from court-led interoperability, triage, AI literacy and open legal data to UPL reform, regulatory sandboxes and third-party certification. Some sources are more optimistic about guided self-help, whereas others prioritise provider augmentation or warn that lower litigation costs may intensify claims against underserved people. One source redirects attention to lawyers’ fact-verification workflows rather than access-to-justice outcomes. A substantial portion of the supplied material is bibliography-only, so those sources remain indeterminate and should not be treated as corroboration. No substantive source in this curated selection clearly opposes the principal proposition, but the selection should not be treated as representative of academia generally.

qs.q: The time has come to appreciate that, although progress on all three fronts is necessary for closing the justice gap and maximizing fairness, it is insufficient if there is not also some level of shared commitment and coordination across—and not just within—all fronts.
qs.a: Interoperable Legal AI for Access to Justice · Academia · 2025

vlens.an: Within this curated set, regulators, courts and professional bodies generally accept the proposition’s distinction between making legal guidance cheaper or more available and securing effective remedies. Their common reasons are that access claims remain largely prospective; consumer-facing systems may provide inaccurate information or fabricated authorities; unaided use raises verification and unauthorized-practice concerns; and digital or institutional inequalities may concentrate benefits. Several sources therefore distinguish risky consumer self-help from provider augmentation, which may expand legal-aid capacity but requires trustworthy systems, human fallback, funding and shared infrastructure. Material variation remains: the 2025 access-to-justice report builds on the proposition with concrete deployment and infrastructure proposals, while McCormack’s contribution takes the contrary, predictive view that AI-enabled dispute resolution can improve fairness, reduce docket burdens and extend effective justice. Two sources are indeterminate because the supplied excerpts are bibliographic rather than substantive. These positions describe only the selected sources and should not be treated as representative of the wider professional group.

qs.q: According to a January 2024 study by researchers from Stanford University,55  popular AI chatbots, such as Open AI’s ChatGPT3.5, Google’s PaLM 2 and Meta’s Llama 2, are  inaccurate in the majority of cases when answering legal questions, posing special risks for people  relying on the technology because they can’t afford a human lawyer.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations of the New York State Bar Association Task Force on Artificial Intelligence (April 2024) · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Without targeted funding and shared infrastructure, legal services organizations risk diverging into a two- tiered system where some scale exponentially while others fall behind.
qs.a: Report and Recommendations on Artificial Intelligence and Access to Justice in 2025 · Regulators & courts · 2026

elens.an: The substantive 2015–2022 evidence accepts the proposition’s underlying distinction between expanding legal-AI availability and achieving meaningful access to justice, then materially develops it through a distributional and institutional account. Simshaw does not provide the later federal-filing evidence about increased self-representation or establish whether cheaper assistance improves remedies. Instead, he argues that potential benefits—self-help, information, intake and connections to professionals—depend on the consumer, legal issue and process, and may otherwise produce inferior services for poorer users, concentrate effective AI among expensive firms or leave affordability barriers unchanged. His concrete extension is a framework of context-sensitive calibration, supported by regulated experimentation and cross-field collaboration. Internal variation is primarily evidentiary: Simshaw offers a clear constructive position, whereas the supplied excerpt from the legal-technologies survey contains only acknowledgements and funding provenance, so its position is indeterminate. Because the corpus is curated, this contrast should not be treated as indicating the prevalence of either view during the period.

qs.q: Legal AI’s Promise: Tools to Help Close the Justice Gap         Legal AI is on the rise, but the availability of legal services is not.
qs.a: Access to A.I. Justice: Avoiding an Inequitable Two-Tiered System of Legal Services · Academia · 2022

qs.q: Part III provides a taxonomy of important considerations that stakeholders face when working to “calibrate” an appropriate level of AI use in light of the specific consumers, legal issues, and underlying processes involved, and argues that this calibration is key to avoiding a two-tiered system.
qs.a: Access to A.I. Justice: Avoiding an Inequitable Two-Tiered System of Legal Services · Academia · 2022

elens.an: The substantive 2023–2024 sources accept the proposition’s central distinction: cheaper or more accessible AI assistance may widen access to legal information and participation, but that does not establish effective remedies or improved outcomes. Their common reasons are that access claims remain prospective; generic chatbots and even specialised tools can produce inaccurate information or fabricated citations; unaided users may be especially vulnerable; digital and economic inequalities can distribute benefits unevenly; and unauthorized-practice rules complicate consumer-facing deployment. The period materially builds on the proposition by proposing concrete responses rather than merely restating its caution: human-centred design and research, support for legal-aid providers, court and process adaptation, better longitudinal outcome data, reconsideration of UPL restrictions with consumer safeguards, and certification of legal AI assistants. Material internal variation concerns the preferred pathway. Some sources emphasise trustworthy self-help and basic legal information; others favour provider augmentation or court-led systems. Walters prioritises calibrated UPL reform, while Bonardi and Branting outline third-party certification and exemptions. Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice stresses unequal effects, judicial adaptation and outcome measurement. More optimistic commentary presents digitisation as potentially democratising law but supplies no evidence on remedies, so its relation to the proposition remains unclear rather than contrary. Several other records are bibliographic only and cannot establish a position. No supplied substantive source clearly rejects the proposition, but the curated set should not be treated as representative or its source counts as evidence of prevalence.

qs.q: While legal tech will bring many            beneﬁts and may even help to level the playing ﬁeld in certain respects, some of            the more potent and immediately available tools will likely tilt the playing ﬁeld,            skewing it ever further toward powerful players.
qs.a: Legal Tech and the Future of Civil Justice · Academia · 2023

qs.q: Considering the potential benefit to consumers, state legislatures should re-evaluate the scope of UPL laws in order to expand assistance while still protecting consumers from negligent or fraudulent legal services.
qs.a: Re-Regulating UPL in an Age of AI · Academia · 2024

elens.an: The substantively available 2025 sources broadly support the cluster’s principal proposition: lower-cost GenAI can increase legal information, drafting capacity, self-help and provider productivity, but those forms of assistance do not by themselves establish effective remedies or population-level access gains. Common reasons include users’ difficulty recognising and pursuing legal claims, limited ability to verify AI output, hallucination and misinformation risks, digital and informational inequality, and the possibility that cheaper legal action shifts screening costs to courts or strengthens sophisticated repeat litigants. Several sources materially develop the practical response through legal-aid augmentation, trained justice-tech intermediaries, verification requirements, community-centred design, targeted regulatory reform and court-led interoperability. Internal variation is substantial: Bibas places greater weight on reducing delivery costs through procedural and bar-regulatory reform; Fines favours guided self-help and relaxed UPL restrictions; Markovic stresses adversarial distributional risks; and Simshaw prioritises coordination across consumers, providers and courts. McCormack offers the clearest contrary view, predicting that responsibly implemented AI dispute resolution will itself improve accessibility, fairness and institutional efficiency, but the supplied passage is prospective rather than outcome evidence. Bibliography-only or fragmentary sources remain indeterminate and should not be treated as supporting either side. Because this is a curated selection, these alignments indicate relationships among the supplied sources, not prevalence across 2025 commentary generally.

elens.an:
The substantive 2026 sources broadly accept the cluster’s principal proposition that cheaper GenAI assistance can increase participation without ensuring effective remedies, and materially extend it in three ways. First, federal-court studies associate the GenAI period with sharply increased self-representation while finding either worse outcomes for AI-flagged complaints or little change in case quality and resolution speed; neither design, as supplied, conclusively establishes that AI caused the filing increase. Second, they propose mechanisms and institutional consequences: lower drafting friction may admit marginal claims, displace professional pre-filing screening and transfer work to judges, staff and defendants. Third, provider- and court-side sources develop a practical alternative to unaided consumer substitution through task-specific professional augmentation, court adaptation, citation verification, legal-data infrastructure, targeted funding and human fallback.

Material variation remains. Cohen-Sasson reports more dismissals and no greater access to remedy, whereas Shah and Levy find little apparent change in quality rather than clear deterioration; these concern different comparisons and are not direct contradictions. Public-defense interview evidence locates AI’s strongest potential in evidence investigation and its weakest fit in courtroom representation and strategy, but does not demonstrate productivity or client-outcome gains. The access-to-justice report is more optimistic about scaling legal aid and consumer tools, yet conditions that prospect on safeguards, funding and shared infrastructure and supplies mainly recommendations rather than quantified remedy outcomes. The fact-verification study redirects attention from self-representation to how AI reshapes lawyers’ judgment and responsibility. Numerous other records are bibliographic or fragmentary, so their positions remain indeterminate and should not be treated as contrary evidence. Because this is a curated corpus, these relationships describe the supplied sources only and do not establish prevalence among researchers or practitioners.

qs.q: First, move beyond the human–machine dichotomy and design interfaces that make humans and AI more effec- tive together.
